intro: Martial arts carry names, and names can be claimed. A Kodokan certificate, a Kukkiwon registry number, a U.S. trademark and a UNESCO heritage listing each say that someone holds a name. Sometimes those records agree. Sometimes, as with the several groups that have called themselves the International Taekwon-Do Federation since 2002, they point in different directions.

Martial arts also carry memory. Karate grew in the Ryukyu Kingdom before Japan annexed it in 1879. Brazil's 1890 penal code made capoeira a crime two years after slavery ended. Japanese American judo clubs met inside incarceration camps after 1942. Women and Black athletes waited decades for the titles and ranks their skill had earned.

In this unit you will weigh dated records against legends and feelings. You will read laws, court cases, rank registers and heritage lists as evidence. By the end, you will be able to argue who holds a martial art's name, and how a school can honor its founders while telling hard history factually.
bigQuestion: Who has the right to claim a martial art's name and its past, and what evidence should decide?

title: Ownership

chapters.title: Who Owns a Name
chapters.bigQuestion: When two groups claim the same martial art name, which records can settle who holds it, and which records cannot?

story.title: Three Letters on a Door
story.kicker: A lawyer and a teacher read the same sign on a school door in two different ways.
paragraphs: A small taekwondo school sits between a bakery and a tax office. Painted on its glass door are three letters: ITF. Below them is the teacher's name and a phone number. One evening a lawyer stops by. She is helping a client open a new school across town, and her client wants to use the same three letters.

The teacher points to a framed certificate on the wall. It is signed by an officer of the International Taekwon-Do Federation. "These letters belong to the federation that promoted me," he says. The lawyer nods, then explains a problem. Since 2002, several different groups have each called themselves the International Taekwon-Do Federation. Each one issues its own certificates.

"So which group owns the letters?" the teacher asks. The lawyer says it depends on the question. A trademark office keeps one kind of record. A federation keeps another kind in its rank register. A founder's writings, a court ruling and a newspaper story are each a different kind of evidence.

They sit down at the front desk. The teacher opens a binder of old tournament programs. The lawyer opens a laptop to a public trademark search. For the next hour, they do not argue about who is the better teacher. They argue about which papers answer which question.
story.think: The teacher and the lawyer look at different records. What question can each kind of record answer?

lessons.title: Scrolls in the Old Schools
lessons.mainIdea: In early modern Japan, a martial school's head controlled its name by granting written licenses, such as the menkyo kaiden.
reading: In Japan before 1868, many martial traditions were organized as a *ryū*, a school with its own name, founder story and line of heads. A ryū might teach swordsmanship, archery or unarmed arts. Membership was often tied to a domain or a family. The school's name was a kind of property that its head protected.

A ryū marked a student's progress with written scrolls called licenses. The highest was often the *menkyo kaiden*, meaning "license of complete transmission." It stated that the holder had received the full teaching of that school. A person holding it could often teach and pass the school's name on.

A related pattern, the *iemoto* system, grew in Edo-period (1603–1868) arts such as the tea ceremony and flower arranging. In it, one head of a family line holds final authority over licenses. Historians note that license fees could help support a school's head. The same idea of a chain of permission shaped several martial schools.

words.d: a named Japanese school or tradition with its own line of heads
"license of complete transmission"; the top written license in many old Japanese schools
a system in which one family head holds final authority over a school's licenses
a line of teachers and students through which a school's name passes

lessons.title: Kanō's Numbered Ranks
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō Jigorō's Kodokan replaced scroll licenses with numbered dan grades recorded in its own register, a model many arts later copied.
reading: In 1882, Kanō Jigorō opened the *Kodokan* in a room at Eishō-ji, a Buddhist temple in Tokyo. He had studied older jujutsu schools. He wanted a school that fit a modern country with public schools and written rules. The Kodokan kept careful records of every student who joined.

In 1883, Kanō gave the first *dan* grades to two students, Saigō Shirō and Tomita Tsunejirō. A dan is a numbered grade, counted upward from first dan. Unlike a scroll written for one student, a numbered rank could be compared across hundreds of students. The Kodokan kept each promotion in its register.

Colored belts for beginners came later. Kawaishi Mikinosuke, a Japanese teacher who moved to France in the 1930s, is widely credited with spreading a system of many colors for the grades below dan, called *kyū*. Today a Kodokan certificate is still a record that anyone can ask the Kodokan to confirm.

words.d: the judo school and headquarters Kanō Jigorō founded in Tokyo in 1882
a numbered rank counted upward from first dan
a grade below the dan ranks, often shown by colored belts

check.q: What made a numbered dan rank different from an old scroll license?

lessons.title: A Registry in Seoul
lessons.mainIdea: The Kukkiwon in Seoul, founded in 1972, issues taekwondo dan and poom certificates to students in many countries and keeps them in one registry.
reading: The *Kukkiwon* is a large hall in the Gangnam district of Seoul. Its building was finished in November 1972. The Korean government backed it as a central home for taekwondo. The name is often translated as "national gymnasium" or "national technique hall."

The Kukkiwon issues rank certificates for taekwondo. Adults receive dan ranks. Students under fifteen receive *poom* ranks, a junior form of black-belt rank that can be changed to dan later. A school anywhere in the world can apply to register its students. Each certificate carries a number that can be checked in the Kukkiwon's records.

A central registry changes how a teacher proves a claim. A school's owner may say he trained in Korea. A Kukkiwon number is a record another person can look up. Many national taekwondo bodies and the World Taekwondo federation accept Kukkiwon ranks. Schools linked to the separate International Taekwon-Do Federation use their own certificates instead.

words.d: the taekwondo headquarters in Seoul, finished in 1972, that issues dan and poom certificates
a junior black-belt rank in taekwondo for students under fifteen
an official list that records who holds which rank or right

check.why: A numbered certificate can be checked in the Kukkiwon's records by someone else.

lessons.title: What a Trademark Can Hold
lessons.mainIdea: A trademark protects a brand name for a business, but the general name of an art, such as judo or karate, cannot be owned.
reading: In the United States, the Lanham Act of 1946 is the main federal law on trademarks. A *trademark* is a word, name or symbol that tells buyers who offers a product or service. The United States Patent and Trademark Office keeps the federal register. A school can register its own name, logo or a special program title.

Trademark law will not let anyone own a *generic* word. A generic word is the common name for a whole kind of thing. "Karate," "judo" and "boxing" are generic names of arts. A company could register "Maple Street Karate," but not the word karate by itself. That rule keeps the name of a shared practice open to everyone.

Family names can become brands, and that can cause conflict. In Brazil, the Gracie family became well known for Brazilian jiu-jitsu, a grappling art that grew from judo taught there in the early 1900s. In the United States in the 1990s, members of the Gracie family went to court over who could use the family name on schools. The case shows that a lineage name can also be a business name.

words.d: a word, name or symbol that shows who offers a product or service
the common name for a whole kind of thing, which no one can own as a trademark
the 1946 United States law that governs federal trademarks

lessons.title: A Word the Olympic Movement Owns
lessons.mainIdea: A 1978 federal law gave the U.S. Olympic Committee control of the word Olympic, and the Supreme Court upheld that control in 1987.
reading: Congress passed the *Amateur Sports Act* in 1978. The law organized amateur sport in the United States under the U.S. Olympic Committee. It also gave the committee the right to control commercial use of the word "Olympic" and the five rings. In 1998, Congress renamed it the Ted Stevens Olympic and Amateur Sports Act.

In the early 1980s, a San Francisco group planned an event called the "Gay Olympic Games." The U.S. Olympic Committee sued to stop the use of the word. In 1987, in San Francisco Arts and Athletics v. United States Olympic Committee, the Supreme Court ruled for the committee. The event went ahead in 1982 under the name Gay Games.

The case matters for martial arts because Olympic arts carry an extra name. Judo joined the Olympic program in 1964 and taekwondo became a medal sport in 2000. A school may teach Olympic-style judo, but using the word Olympic in a brand can raise legal questions. Here, ownership of a word comes from a statute, not from a lineage or a founder.

words.d: the 1978 U.S. law that organized amateur sport and gave the Olympic Committee control of the word Olympic
a written law passed by a legislature such as Congress
the highest court in the United States

look.title: What the Law Protects
look.text: The law gives the U.S. Olympic Committee the exclusive right to use the word Olympic and the five-ring symbol, and lets it sue anyone who uses them to sell goods or promote a competition without permission.

look.prompt: Who holds the right to the word here? How is that different from a family or a federation holding a name?

choices: the right to run the Kodokan

check.why: The 1978 law gave the committee control of commercial use of the word Olympic and the five rings.

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in 1987 in San Francisco Arts and Athletics v. USOC?
choices: It ruled for the U.S. Olympic Committee.

check.why: The Supreme Court ruled for the U.S. Olympic Committee in 1987.

check.q: Where does the Olympic committee's right to the word come from?
check.why: The right comes from a federal statute, the Amateur Sports Act.

lessons.title: Three Letters, Many Owners
lessons.mainIdea: Taekwondo has two major federations, and after its founder's death in 2002 the ITF split into several groups that each use the same name.
reading: Choi Hong-hi, a South Korean army general, founded the *International Taekwon-Do Federation* (ITF) in Seoul in 1966. He clashed with the South Korean government. In 1972 he moved to Canada and took the ITF's headquarters to Toronto. He later built ties with North Korea.

In 1973, a separate body, the World Taekwondo Federation, was founded in Seoul with South Korean government support. It led the path to the Olympics. Taekwondo was a demonstration sport in 1988 and 1992 and a full medal sport in 2000. In 2017 the federation shortened its name to *World Taekwondo*.

Choi died in Pyongyang, North Korea, in 2002. Soon after, the ITF divided into several rival groups. Each kept the name International Taekwon-Do Federation and each issues its own ranks. A student today may hold an "ITF" certificate from one group that another group does not accept. The name stayed the same while the owners multiplied.

words.d: the taekwondo body Choi Hong-hi founded in Seoul in 1966, later split into rival groups
the international federation founded in Seoul in 1973 that governs Olympic taekwondo
an organization that joins many schools or national groups under shared rules
competing with another group for the same thing

check.why: General Choi Hong-hi founded the ITF in Seoul in 1966.

check.why: After Choi's death in 2002, the ITF divided into several groups that each kept the name.

check.why: Taekwondo was a demonstration sport in 1988 and 1992 and became a medal sport in 2000.

sections.title: A Nation Puts Its Name On

lessons.title: Naming Taekwondo
lessons.mainIdea: Taekwondo received its name in 1955 and became an official symbol of South Korea through federations, a national park and a 2018 law.
reading: After Japanese colonial rule ended in 1945, several schools called *kwan* opened in Seoul. Each kwan used its own name for its art. In 1955, Korean teachers and officials agreed on a single name: taekwondo. Choi Hong-hi is widely credited with proposing it. The name joins three Korean words, often translated as foot, fist and way.

The Korea Taekwondo Association, founded in 1959, worked to bring the kwan under one national body. Unifying the schools took years. The government saw a shared national art as useful for military training, for schools and for showing Korea to the world. Taekwondo demonstration teams toured abroad in the 1960s and 1970s.

The state's role grew over time. A national taekwondo park called Taekwondowon opened in 2014 in Muju County. In 2018, South Korea's National Assembly passed a law naming taekwondo the country's *national sport*. A name that began as a choice among teachers became a legal symbol of a nation.

words.d: a Korean word for a hall or school; used for the first taekwondo schools after 1945
a sport a country names by law or custom as a symbol of itself
the image a country presents to the world through symbols it chooses, such as a sport

look.title: Many Signs, One Word
look.text: Picture a Seoul street in 1953. Five schools have signs with five different names for their art. Now picture the same street in 1975. Most signs now say taekwondo, and many show a national association emblem.
look.prompt: What forces might have changed the signs? Who gained and who lost when one name replaced five?

check.q: In what year did Korean teachers and officials agree on the name taekwondo?
check.why: The name taekwondo was agreed on in 1955.

check.q: What did South Korea's National Assembly do in 2018?
choices: It moved the ITF to Toronto.
It passed a law naming taekwondo the national sport.
check.why: In 2018 the National Assembly passed a law naming taekwondo the national sport.

check.q: What was a kwan in the years after 1945?
choices: a Korean school or hall for the art
check.why: Kwan were the first schools that opened in Seoul after 1945.

lessons.title: Muay Thai and the Thai State
lessons.mainIdea: Thailand links Muay Thai to national history through an honored legend, state-backed stadiums and a federation that won full IOC recognition in 2021.
reading: Thai tradition tells of Nai Khanom Tom, a fighter captured by Burmese forces after the fall of Ayutthaya in 1767. In the story, he wins his freedom by defeating many opponents before a Burmese king. The account comes from later chronicles and is best read as a *legend*. Thailand marks March 17 as National Muay Thai Day in his honor.

In the twentieth century, Bangkok's two great stadiums became national stages. Rajadamnern Stadium opened in 1945. Lumpinee Stadium opened in 1956 and was run by the Royal Thai Army. Fight nights at these stadiums were broadcast across the country. The name "Muay Thai," meaning Thai boxing, tied the sport to the nation itself.

The International Federation of Muaythai Associations (IFMA) was founded in 1992 to organize amateur Muay Thai worldwide. The International Olympic Committee gave IFMA provisional *recognition* in 2016 and full recognition in 2021. Recognition does not put a sport on the Olympic program. It does mean the IOC accepts IFMA as the sport's world governing body.

words.d: a traditional story about the past that cannot be fully checked in records
the IOC's formal acceptance of a group as a sport's world governing body
the International Federation of Muaythai Associations, founded in 1992

look.cite: International Federation of Muaythai Associations history; International Olympic Committee records
look.prompt: How many years passed between provisional and full IOC recognition?

check.q: How should a historian treat the story of Nai Khanom Tom?
choices: as a legend from later chronicles
check.why: The Nai Khanom Tom account comes from later chronicles and is best read as a legend.

check.q: Which Bangkok stadium was run by the Royal Thai Army?
check.why: Lumpinee Stadium, opened in 1956, was run by the Royal Thai Army.

check.q: What did IOC recognition of IFMA in 2021 mean?
choices: The IOC accepts IFMA as Muay Thai's world governing body.

check.why: Recognition means the IOC accepts IFMA as the governing body; it does not add the sport to the Games.

lessons.title: Heritage Lists and Shared Names
lessons.mainIdea: UNESCO's heritage lists let nations name martial practices as their living heritage, and sometimes two nations claim related arts.
reading: In 2003, UNESCO adopted the Convention for the Safeguarding of the *Intangible Cultural Heritage*. Intangible heritage means living practices, such as songs, festivals and crafts, rather than buildings. Countries nominate practices for UNESCO's lists. A place on the list is a statement by a nation about what belongs to its people.

Several martial practices are on the list. Iran's pahlevani and zoorkhaneh rituals and Turkey's Kırkpınar oil wrestling festival were added in 2010. Korea's taekkyeon was added in 2011. Brazil's capoeira circle, the roda, was added in 2014. Brazil had already named capoeira national heritage in 2008.

Sometimes a listing shows how names cross borders. In 2018, North Korea and South Korea were jointly inscribed for ssireum, a form of Korean wrestling, the first joint listing by the two states. In 2019, Indonesia's pencak silat and Malaysia's silat were inscribed as two separate entries. Each nation named its own tradition within a family of related arts.

words.d: living practices, such as festivals, songs and crafts, that a community passes on
the United Nations agency for education, science and culture
to add a practice officially to a UNESCO list

lessons.title: Diaspora Rooms
lessons.mainIdea: Migrants carried martial arts to new countries, and diaspora schools kept, changed and renamed those arts far from where they began.
reading: A *diaspora* is a community that lives far from its homeland but keeps ties to it. Japanese immigrants began arriving in Hawaii in large numbers in the 1880s to work on sugar plantations. They built temples, language schools and judo clubs. In 1934, the Okinawan karate teacher Miyagi Chōjun visited Hawaii to teach in the islands' Okinawan community.

Filipino workers came to Hawaii and California in the 1920s and 1930s. Many of them practiced arnis, also called eskrima, a Filipino art. For decades it was taught quietly among friends and family. In 1966, Angel Cabales opened a school in Stockton, California, that is often called the first public eskrima school in the United States.

Brazilian teachers brought capoeira to New York and other U.S. cities in the 1970s. A diaspora school often faces two sets of questions. Elders at home may ask whether it keeps the tradition. New students may ask whether it welcomes them. A school's name, its teacher's lineage and its ties to the homeland all become part of its answer.

words.d: a community living far from its homeland that keeps ties to it
a Filipino martial art, also called eskrima or kali
people moving from one country or region to live in another

look.text: In a Hawaiian plantation town, a Buddhist temple hall is used for a Japanese-language school in the afternoon. On weekday evenings the chairs are stacked and mats are laid down for a judo club. Photographs of teachers from Japan hang on the wall.
look.prompt: What does this shared room tell you about how a diaspora community kept its practices?

choices: a community living far from its homeland that keeps ties to it
check.why: A diaspora is a community far from its homeland that keeps ties to it.

check.why: Miyagi Chōjun visited Hawaii in 1934 to teach in the Okinawan community.

check.q: Where did Angel Cabales open his eskrima school in 1966?
check.why: Angel Cabales opened his school in Stockton, California, in 1966.

lessons.title: Evidence, Not a Feeling
lessons.mainIdea: Strong claims about a name rest on dated records, such as the 1936 Naha meeting that chose the written name for karate.
reading: The word karate was once written with characters meaning "Chinese hand." On October 25, 1936, leading Okinawan teachers met in Naha at a meeting hosted by a local newspaper. They agreed to use characters meaning "empty hand" instead. The newspaper printed a report of the meeting. In 2005, the Okinawa Prefectural Assembly named October 25 as Karate Day.

That meeting is strong *evidence* because it has a date, a place, named people and a printed record. Other claims about karate's past rest on family memory. *Oral history*, the memories people tell and record, is valuable, and historians collect it carefully. They also compare it with letters, photographs, newspapers and official registers.

Historians ask the same questions of any claim to a name. Who made the record, and when? Did anyone gain from it? Does a second, independent source agree? A certificate, a trademark, a heritage listing and a legend can all be true in their own way. Each answers a different question about who holds a name.

words.d: records or objects that support a claim about the past
memories that people tell aloud, which historians record and study
a record made by someone separate from the person making a claim

chapters.title: Memory in the Gym
chapters.bigQuestion: How did empire, occupation and exclusion shape martial arts, and how can a school tell that history honestly on its walls?

story.title: A Photograph Above a Flag
story.kicker: A student notices that a founder's portrait hangs above a flag he never saw.
paragraphs: In a karate school in a suburb of Chicago, the front wall holds three things. In the middle is a black-and-white photograph of Funakoshi Gichin, an Okinawan teacher who brought karate to Tokyo in 1922. Below it hang two flags: the flag of the United States and the flag of Japan.

A high school student named Dana stays after class to help stack mats. She reads the small card under the photo. It says Funakoshi was born in 1868 in Shuri. That town was then the royal capital of the Ryukyu Kingdom. Japan did not take over the kingdom until 1879, when Funakoshi was a boy.

Dana asks the owner a question. "Did he ever come to America?" The owner shakes his head. Funakoshi never visited the United States. He died in Tokyo in 1957. The American flag is on the wall because the school is in America. The Japanese flag is there because the school's lineage runs through Tokyo.

Dana thinks about what is missing. There is no Ryukyu flag, no map of Okinawa, and no line about the kingdom Funakoshi was born into. She asks whether she can write a longer card for the photo. The owner says yes, if every sentence on it comes with a date and a source.
story.think: What would you put on a card under a founder's photograph so it tells the whole story honestly?

lessons.title: From Ryukyu Kingdom to Okinawa
lessons.mainIdea: Karate grew in the Ryukyu Kingdom, which Japan annexed in 1879, so its history belongs first to Okinawa and not to Japan as a whole.
reading: The *Ryukyu Kingdom* ruled the islands south of Japan from the 1400s. Its capital was Shuri, on Okinawa. The kingdom traded with China and sent tribute missions to the Chinese court. In 1609, armies from the Japanese domain of Satsuma invaded and forced the kingdom to answer to Satsuma as well.

In 1879, the Japanese government ended the kingdom. It made the islands Okinawa Prefecture and moved the last king, Shō Tai, to Tokyo. This takeover is called an *annexation*. Okinawan schools began teaching in Japanese. Local customs, dress and language came under pressure to change.

Karate grew in Shuri, Naha and Tomari, towns of the old kingdom. Teachers there drew on local practice and on ties with China. When karate reached mainland Japan in the 1920s, it arrived as an art from a recently annexed place. Historians therefore describe early karate as Okinawan, or Ryukyuan, rather than simply Japanese.

words.d: the island kingdom centered on Okinawa, ended by Japan in 1879
when one country takes over another territory and makes it part of itself
a state that rules other lands and peoples, often by force
gifts or payments a smaller state sent to a stronger one to show loyalty

check.why: Karate grew in Shuri, Naha and Tomari, towns of the old Ryukyu Kingdom.

lessons.title: A Hall for the Empire
lessons.mainIdea: The Dai Nippon Butokukai, founded in 1895, tied martial arts to the Japanese state until the Allied occupation dissolved it in 1946.
reading: The *Dai Nippon Butokukai*, or Greater Japan Martial Virtue Society, was founded in Kyoto in 1895. That was the year Japan won its war with China. In 1899, the society opened a large hall, the Butokuden, near Heian Shrine in Kyoto. It held yearly demonstrations and awarded teaching titles.

The Butokukai grew into a national body with branches across Japan and in lands Japan ruled. It set standards for kendo, judo and other arts. In 1942, during the Second World War, the government reorganized it under state control. Its work became part of wartime training and national spirit campaigns.

After Japan's defeat in 1945, Allied officials saw the society as part of the wartime state. The Butokukai was dissolved in 1946, and many of its leaders were barred from public posts. Its story shows how a society for traditional arts could become a tool of an *empire*. Later groups used the same name, but they are separate organizations.

words.d: the Greater Japan Martial Virtue Society, founded in Kyoto in 1895 and dissolved in 1946
the Butokukai's demonstration hall in Kyoto, opened in 1899
to officially end an organization

look.prompt: What should a plaque on this building say about both periods? Why might people disagree?

check.why: The Butokukai was founded in Kyoto in 1895.

choices: They saw it as part of Japan's wartime state.
check.why: After 1945, Allied officials saw the society as part of the wartime state and dissolved it.

check.q: What happened to the Butokukai in 1942?
choices: The government reorganized it under state control.
check.why: In 1942 the government reorganized the Butokukai under state control.

lessons.title: Korea Under Colonial Rule
lessons.mainIdea: Japan ruled Korea from 1910 to 1945, and many founders of the first taekwondo schools had trained in Japanese karate during those years.
reading: Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled it as a *colony* until 1945. Colonial schools taught in Japanese, and in the late 1930s Koreans were pressured to take Japanese names. Judo and kendo were taught in schools and police training. Many Korean students also went to Japan for university.

Several founders of the first Korean schools, the kwan, trained in karate while studying or working in Japan. Lee Won-kuk, for example, trained in Tokyo and opened Chung Do Kwan in Seoul in 1944. After liberation in 1945, these teachers built new schools. Over time, they changed names, forms and rules to make an art they saw as Korean.

Some official histories of taekwondo stress much older roots, such as Goguryeo tomb paintings and the Silla hwarang, a group of young elites. Historians agree those ancient sources exist. Many argue that modern taekwondo's direct roots run through karate learned during the colonial era. Holding both facts helps explain why the art's national story matters so much in Korea.

words.d: a land ruled by another country
Korea's freedom from Japanese rule in August 1945
a group of young elites in the ancient Korean kingdom of Silla

check.why: Many historians trace modern taekwondo's direct roots to karate learned during colonial rule.

lessons.title: Capoeira and the 1890 Penal Code
lessons.mainIdea: Two years after Brazil ended slavery in 1888, its 1890 penal code made capoeira a crime, and schools only became legal in the 1930s.
reading: Capoeira is an Afro-Brazilian art that grew among enslaved Africans and their descendants in Brazil. Brazil abolished slavery on May 13, 1888, with the Golden Law. It was the last country in the Americas to do so. Freed people faced poverty, police control and laws aimed at their gatherings.

In 1890, Brazil's first republican *penal code* made capoeira a crime. Its chapter on "vagrants and capoeiras" set prison terms for practicing it in streets and public squares. Police arrested practitioners for decades. The law targeted a practice linked to Black Brazilians just after emancipation.

Change came in the 1930s. In 1937, Manoel dos Reis Machado, known as Mestre Bimba, received official approval for his academy in Salvador, Bahia. In 1941, Vicente Ferreira Pastinha, known as Mestre Pastinha, opened a center for capoeira Angola. Brazil's new penal code of 1940 left capoeira out. In 2014 UNESCO listed the capoeira circle as heritage.

words.d: a set of laws that defines crimes and punishments
the legal end of slavery; in Brazil, the Golden Law of 1888
from the history and culture of Brazilians of African descent
Portuguese for master; a title for a senior capoeira teacher

check.why: The 1890 code set prison terms for practicing capoeira in streets and public squares.

check.why: Manoel dos Reis Machado, Mestre Bimba, received official approval for his academy in 1937.

lessons.title: The Occupation of Japan
lessons.mainIdea: During the Allied occupation from 1945 to 1952, martial arts were removed from Japanese schools, then returned in new forms as sport.
reading: Japan surrendered in August 1945. Allied forces, led by the United States, then governed the country until 1952. This period is called the *occupation*. Occupation officials worked to remove wartime nationalism from schools, and school martial arts were stopped in late 1945.

Judo leaders argued that judo was a sport, not military training. The All Japan Judo Federation was founded in 1949, and judo returned to school programs in 1950. Kendo came back more slowly. The All Japan Kendo Federation was founded in 1952, the year the occupation ended.

The return reshaped the arts as *sport*, with federations, rule books and national championships. In 1964, Tokyo hosted the Olympic Games, and judo appeared on the program for the first time. The Nippon Budokan hall was built for the judo events. Anton Geesink of the Netherlands won the open-weight gold medal.

words.d: when a foreign power governs a country after a war; in Japan, 1945 to 1952
strong loyalty to one's nation, sometimes used to support war
a physical contest organized with rule books, federations and championships

lessons.title: Judo Behind Barbed Wire
lessons.mainIdea: After 1942, the U.S. government forced about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry into camps, where many kept judo and sumo clubs going.
reading: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. Within days, the FBI arrested hundreds of Japanese American community leaders. Teachers of judo and kendo were among those detained, partly because their clubs had ties to groups in Japan. No evidence showed that these teachers were spies.

On February 19, 1942, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed *Executive Order 9066*. It led to the forced removal of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry from the West Coast. About two-thirds were U.S. citizens. They were held in ten camps run by the War Relocation Authority, surrounded by barbed wire and guard towers.

Inside the camps, people built schools, churches, newspapers and sports clubs. Judo and sumo clubs met in barracks and open lots. After the camps closed, thousands of Japanese Americans moved to Chicago to start over. In 1988, the Civil Liberties Act gave a formal U.S. apology and 20,000 dollars to each surviving person who had been held. This forced removal is called *incarceration*.

words.d: the 1942 order that led to the forced removal of Japanese Americans from the West Coast
being locked up and held against one's will
the 1988 U.S. law that apologized for the camps and paid survivors

look.prompt: What does this photo show about how people kept community life going? What does the guard tower remind you to include in a caption?

lessons.title: Women Left Out of the Bracket
lessons.mainIdea: Women trained in judo from the 1920s, but they waited until 1980 for a world championship and until 1992 for Olympic medals.
reading: The Kodokan opened a formal women's section, the *Joshi-bu*, in 1926. Women had trained with Kanō Jigorō's support before that. For decades, though, women's judo focused on forms and training, not contests. Their ranks and titles were often limited compared with men's.

Rena "Rusty" Kanokogi of Brooklyn, New York, entered a YMCA judo tournament in 1959. She won, but officials took her medal when they learned she was a woman. She spent the next years pushing for women's contests. In 1980, she organized the first women's world judo championships, held at Madison Square Garden in New York.

Women's judo was a demonstration event at the 1988 Seoul Olympics. Women first won Olympic judo medals at the 1992 Barcelona Games. Title IX, the 1972 U.S. law against sex discrimination in schools that receive federal money, helped open college and school programs. The medals on today's walls show only the years after the doors opened.

words.d: the Kodokan's women's section, formally opened in 1926
unfair treatment of people because of who they are
the 1972 U.S. law banning sex discrimination in schools that receive federal money

check.why: Officials took her medal when they learned she was a woman.

choices: Madison Square Garden in New York
check.why: Kanokogi organized the 1980 championships at Madison Square Garden.

check.q: When did women first win Olympic judo medals?
check.why: Women's judo was a demonstration in 1988; medals came at the 1992 Barcelona Games.

lessons.title: Keiko Fukuda's Long Climb
lessons.mainIdea: Keiko Fukuda began judo in 1935 and reached the highest rank only in 2011, showing how slowly rank systems opened to women.
reading: Keiko Fukuda was born in Tokyo in 1913. Her grandfather, Fukuda Hachinosuke, had taught Tenjin Shin'yō-ryū jujutsu to a young Kanō Jigorō. In 1935, Kanō invited her to train at the Kodokan's women's section. She became a teacher there and spent her life in judo.

For many years, the Kodokan limited how high women could rise in rank. Fukuda was held at fifth dan for about three decades. In 1972, after public pressure, she became one of the first two women promoted to sixth dan. She had moved to the United States in the 1960s and taught for decades in the San Francisco Bay Area.

In 2006, the Kodokan promoted Fukuda to ninth dan. In 2011, USA Judo and the U.S. Judo Federation awarded her tenth dan, the highest *rank*. She died in 2013 at age 99. Her record shows that a rank list is also a record of who was allowed to climb it, and when.

words.d: a level in a system that shows a person's standing, such as a dan grade
being raised to a higher rank
the national governing body for judo in the United States

look.prompt: What does this list tell you about skill, and what does it tell you about rules? How would you caption it?

check.why: In 1972 Fukuda became one of the first two women the Kodokan promoted to sixth dan.

check.q: Who awarded Fukuda tenth dan in 2011?

check.why: USA Judo and the U.S. Judo Federation awarded her tenth dan in 2011.

lessons.title: A Champion Pardoned Late
lessons.mainIdea: Jack Johnson, the first Black world heavyweight boxing champion, was convicted under a racist prosecution in 1913 and pardoned only in 2018.
reading: In the late 1800s, white heavyweight champions refused to fight Black challengers. This barrier was called the *color line*. John L. Sullivan, champion from 1882, openly drew it. Black boxers could win lesser titles but were kept from the heavyweight championship.

Jack Johnson, born in Galveston, Texas, in 1878, broke the line. On December 26, 1908, in Sydney, Australia, he beat Tommy Burns for the world heavyweight title. On July 4, 1910, in Reno, Nevada, he beat former champion James Jeffries. White mobs attacked Black Americans in many cities after that fight.

Johnson lived in Chicago and opened a nightclub there in 1912. In 1913, an all-white jury convicted him under the Mann Act, a law used against him because of his relationships with white women. He later served about a year in federal prison. In 2018, he received a posthumous *pardon*, 72 years after his death.

words.d: a barrier that kept Black athletes out of contests or titles
an official act that forgives a crime; posthumous means after death
a 1910 U.S. law that was used to prosecute Jack Johnson in 1913

choices: a painted line on the ring floor

check.why: The color line was the barrier white champions used to refuse Black challengers.

check.why: Johnson was pardoned in 2018, 72 years after his death.

lessons.title: A Founder and a Lost Games
lessons.mainIdea: Kanō Jigorō won the 1940 Olympics for Tokyo, but Japan's war with China led it to give up the Games in 1938, the year he died.
reading: In 1909, Kanō Jigorō became the first Asian member of the International Olympic Committee. He led Japan's first Olympic team in 1912 in Stockholm. He worked for decades to bring the Games to Asia. In 1936, at its meeting in Berlin, the IOC awarded the 1940 Summer Olympics to Tokyo.

In July 1937, full-scale war broke out between Japan and China. Many countries questioned holding the Games in a nation at war. Kanō traveled to an IOC meeting in Cairo in 1938 to defend Tokyo's plan. On his way home, he died aboard the ship Hikawa Maru on May 4, 1938.

In July 1938, Japan's government gave up the 1940 Games. They were moved to Helsinki and then canceled because of the Second World War. Tokyo finally hosted the Olympics in 1964, with judo on the program. A fair portrait caption for Kanō can honor his work and still name the *war* that ended his Olympic plan.

words.d: the body that governs the Olympic Games
armed conflict between nations; here Japan's war with China from 1937
the short text beside a photo or object that says what it shows

lessons.title: One Founder, Two Countries
lessons.mainIdea: Choi Hong-hi is honored in some taekwondo schools and left off the walls of others, because his life crossed a divided Korea.
reading: Choi Hong-hi was born in 1918 in the north of Korea, under Japanese rule. He studied in Japan and trained in karate there. After 1945, he became a general in the South Korean army. He founded the International Taekwon-Do Federation in Seoul in 1966 and left South Korea in 1972.

From Canada, Choi built ties with North Korea and helped bring ITF taekwondo there in the 1980s. South Korea's government regarded him as an opponent. He died in Pyongyang in 2002 and was buried there. As a result, *memory* of him differs sharply from one taekwondo school to another.

In many ITF schools, Choi's portrait hangs at the front of the room. In many schools tied to the Kukkiwon and World Taekwondo, his name rarely appears. A careful historian does not choose a side by feeling. The historian lists the dated facts, attributes each view to its group and lets readers see why the wall looks different in each room.

words.d: how a group chooses to remember and honor its past
to say clearly who holds a view or made a claim
the split into North Korea and South Korea after 1945

look.title: Two Walls, One Name

check.q: Why is Choi honored in some schools and not in others?
